head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Table of the key that lies between two keys on a straight line (e.g. 1 and 3 need 2), 0 when nothing lies between
A move is legal when nothing lies between the keys, or the key in between was already used
Every prefix of length at least m is itself a valid pattern, so count it
Symmetry: the 4 corners give equal counts, the 4 edge keys give equal counts, plus the centre
Using symmetry to cut work by about 9x to 3

p: Patterns of exactly L keys (m = n = L). The three starts are a corner (key 1), an edge key (key 2) and the centre (key 5):
bullets: L = 1 gives 9: one pattern per key. For L = 2: 4·5 + 4·7 + 8 = 56.

blocks.h: Why does `used[...]` of the middle key matter?
p: From 1 you may go to 3 only if 2 is already on the pattern, because the line would otherwise pass over it. Knight-like jumps such as 1 to 6 have no key in between, so `skip` is 0 and they are always allowed.

bullets: Time: bounded by the number of patterns (at most 9! = 362,880 orderings), and the symmetry reduces the starts from 9 to 3.
Space: O(9) recursion depth and visited array.

351.takeaway: Backtracking (trying a choice, recursing, then undoing it) with a skip table for jumped-over keys, plus symmetry to run only three starts.

609.takeaway: Group by content with a hash map (defaultdict of lists) and keep groups of size two or more.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each task appears
Count of the most frequent task; it forces the frame length
How many tasks tie for that maximum
(mx − 1) full frames of n + 1 slots, then a last row holding each of the n_max top tasks once
If there are plenty of other tasks, no idle time is needed and the answer is just the task count

p: `A A A B B B`, n = 2:
bullets: Schedule: A B _ A B _ A B (8 slots, two idle).

blocks.h: Why the formula and not a simulation?
p: The most frequent task must be separated by n other slots, so it fixes (mx − 1) frames of width n + 1. Other tasks fill the gaps. If gaps run out, extra tasks simply lengthen the schedule beyond the frame, so the length never drops below `len(tasks)`. Another case: `AAAABBBBCC`, n=1 gives 10 = the task count, with no idle slots.

621.takeaway: Greedy formula: the most frequent task sets the frame (max-1)*(n+1)+ties; answer is the larger of that and the task count.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Python's `heapq` is a min-heap (priority queue returning the smallest item), so negating durations makes the longest course pop first
Total time spent on the courses currently chosen
Deadline missed: drop the longest chosen course, which frees the most time

p: Courses sorted by deadline:

blocks.h: Why drop the longest course, even if it is the new one?
p: Courses are processed in deadline order, so any chosen set fits if its total time meets the current deadline. When it does not, removing one course must restore feasibility, and removing the longest does that while losing only one course. Swapping a long earlier course for a short new one keeps the count the same but leaves more time for later courses.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort and heap operations.

630.takeaway: Sort by deadline, add each course, and when the deadline is missed drop the longest one chosen so far (max-heap via negation).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Exact integer square root (floor), from `math`; avoids float rounding issues of `c ** 0.5`
Two pointers over the sorted range of candidate roots
Two-pointer search in a monotone sum
Increase the sum by raising the small side, decrease it by lowering the big side

blocks.h: Why can pointers only move inward?
p: If `l² + r² < c`, every pair that uses this `l` with any `r' ≤ r` is even smaller, so `l` can be discarded (`l += 1`). If the sum is larger than `c`, every pair using this `r` with any `l' ≥ l` is even larger, so `r` can be discarded (`r -= 1`). Each step removes one candidate, exactly like Two Sum on a sorted array.

633.takeaway: Two pointers from 0 and isqrt(c): the sum of squares is monotone in each pointer.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Call stack of function ids currently running
The time up to which time has already been credited
On a start, credit the interrupted function with the time it ran
End times are inclusive, so the function ran through the whole unit t; +1 counts it
After an end, the parent resumes at the next unit

p: `n = 2`, logs `0:start:0, 1:start:2, 1:end:5, 0:end:6`:

blocks.h: Why `+1` and `prev = t + 1` on end but not on start?
p: A start at time t begins at the beginning of unit t, so the interrupted function ran units prev..t−1 (length t − prev). An end at time t finishes at the end of unit t, so the function ran through unit t (length t − prev + 1), and the next work begins at t + 1.

bullets: Time: O(L) for L log lines.

636.takeaway: Stack of running functions plus a 'credited up to' pointer; ends are inclusive, which is the +1.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of distinct values: the duplicate counted once and the missing number absent
Sum 1..n, the sum when nothing is wrong

blocks.h: Why do these differences give the two values?
p: `sum(nums) − sum(set(nums))` leaves exactly one extra copy of the repeated number. `sum(1..n) − sum(set(nums))` leaves exactly the missing number, since the set has every value 1..n except it. This relies on exactly one value duplicated and one missing.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the set; an in-place sign-marking method uses O(1).

645.takeaway: Arithmetic on sums: duplicate = sum − sum(set), missing = n(n+1)/2 − sum(set).

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Node and everything in its left subtree are too small (BST property), so the answer lies in the right subtree
Pruning a whole subtree by one comparison
In range: keep the node and re-attach the trimmed children

p: BST `[1,0,2]` (1 with left child 0 and right child 2), keep values in [1, 2]:

head: node
decision

0 < 1: discard node and its left subtree, use right
in range: keep, trim both children

bullets: Result: `1(,2)` in `v(left,right)` form: 1 with right child 2.

blocks.h: Why can a whole subtree be skipped?
p: In a BST (Binary Search Tree) all values in a node's left subtree are smaller than the node. If the node is already below `low`, its left subtree is too. The recursion therefore returns the trimmed right subtree directly, and the parent links to it, bypassing the node.

bullets: Time: O(n) worst case, each node visited once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth, h = tree height.

669.takeaway: BST trimming by recursion: out-of-range nodes are replaced by the trimmed subtree on the in-range side.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Smallest possible number of unmatched '(' if every '*' is chosen to help close
Tracking a range of possibilities instead of branching
Largest possible number of unmatched '(' if every '*' is treated as '('
Even with every '*' opening, there are too many ')'
A '*' does not have to close anything, so the count never goes below zero

bullets: Ends with `lo = 0`, so the string is valid (the `*` acts as '(').

p: Every reachable count of open parentheses lies between lo and hi, and every value in between is reachable because each '*' changes the count by at most one in either direction. Only whether 0 lies in [lo, hi] at the end matters, and `hi < 0` at any time kills all options.

bullets: Space: O(1). A stack-based or DP (Dynamic Programming) solution is slower or larger.

678.takeaway: Greedy range [lo, hi] of possible open-parenthesis counts; fail if hi goes negative, succeed if lo ends at 0.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find (disjoint set) forest: each node starts as its own root; index 0 is unused because nodes are numbered from 1
Follows parents to the root, shortening the path as it goes (`parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]`, path halving)
Both ends already connected, so this edge would close a cycle
Cycle detection while building a graph

blocks.h: Why does the first cycle-closing edge give the right answer?
p: The graph has n nodes and n edges, so there is exactly one cycle. Edges are processed in input order, so the edge that first connects two already-connected nodes is the last edge of that cycle in the input, which is what the problem asks for.

bullets: Time: O(n · α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function (practically constant).

684.takeaway: Union-Find (disjoint set): the first edge whose endpoints already share a root is the redundant one.

Extend the child's path only if values match; otherwise the chain restarts at 0
Path bending at node: both arms joined
A path continuing to the parent can use only one arm

p: Tree `[5,4,5,1,1,null,5]`, nodes in post-order:
bullets: The longest path is 5 → 5 → 5 (right side) with 2 edges.

blocks.h: Why `l + 1` and not `l` when the values match?
p: `go` returns the number of edges below the child. Joining the child to the node adds one edge, hence +1. Checking the child's value on the parent (`node.left.val == node.val`) is also what handles a different-valued child whose own chain is long, which must not count.

687.takeaway: Like the tree diameter, but each arm only counts when the child's value equals the node's.

p: Squares that only touch at an edge do not stack. In the example the third square at x = 6 does not overlap anything. Using `<=` would wrongly stack squares that merely share an edge.

blocks.h: Why is the loop `while True` with a lap check?
p: A circular list has no null end to stop on, so the loop stops either when a spot is found or when `cur` returns to `head`. The lap check covers the case where every node has the same value: no ascending pair or wrap point matches, so it is inserted after the last node visited.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sentence → how many times it was typed; a missing key reads as 0
Filters sentences that begin with the prefix
Hot degree descending, then alphabetical (ASCII order) for ties: the tuple key sorts by two criteria, the minus sign flips the first
Ends the sentence: records it and resets the prefix

p: Sentences `i love you` (5), `island` (3), `iroman` (2), `i love leetcode` (2); typing `i`, space, `a`, `#`:

blocks.h: Why scan every sentence instead of using a Trie (prefix tree)?
p: This version is the simplest correct one: each keystroke filters all sentences, O(S·L) per call. A Trie would walk only the prefix path and keep candidates at each node, which wins when the sentence set is large, but takes much more code.

bullets: Time: O(S·L + S log S) per keystroke for S sentences of length L.

642.takeaway: Count map plus filter-and-sort on every keystroke (hot-degree descending, then alphabetical); a Trie is the scalable upgrade.
